chapter: Chicago pioneers, community and New Orleans brotherhood
title: New Orleans players who pine to go home
summary: Armstrong said New Orleans players always want to return; Freddie Kohlman and George Brunis did, and New Orleans musicians work around the clock.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Yeah. I had heard a tape, Pops Foster and Louis Armstrong talking, and I heard it down in New Orleans, New Orleans Jazz Museum. And Louis said the problem with most of the guys from New Orleans was that they always pine to go home again, and they'd go home....
That's why they didn't make it.
No, he didn't go, no. But now, the drummer here --
Right, right. Freddy Kohman, he just had to go back. But he's doing very well down there.
He could have stayed up here, but he was always going back.

They get -- I don't know, they get that kick out of -- like we were saying about brotherhood. Going back and being with their brothers and things like that. And when they get ready, and then when they come away, I mean, they've really had a (unintelligible), because they turn the town out when they come in, and it's one of those things, it's like it was a two-streeted town. Guess who's in town, you know?
Yeah. Well, New Orleans is old-fashioned. That's the way things used to be.
That you didn't need radio and TV.

No, no, no. You had your communication going, you had the communication. And then the guys, if you had a job and couldn't accept, call so-and-so, get so-and-so, he could fill the bill. Yeah, and so -- and then, that's why when they talk about New Orleans music, they work around the clock. They do all kinds of things. They do a funeral early in the morning, and then they'll have an afternoon something and then they'll have a night something.
